newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: OPTUS THREATENS LEGAL ACTION OVER CABLES
The Federal Government is remianing tight-lipped about a reported threat by Optus to take legal action against it, if pay-tv cables have to be moved underground.
Communications Minister, Richard Alston has foreshadowed cables will have to go underground at intersections, and pay-tv companies will need to consult in more detail with local councils.
This follows pressure from the backbench and the community.
With nearly all Optus's cables already above ground, chief executive, Ziggy Switkowski has reportedly warned the Government it'll face legal action if it insists on changing them.
A spokesman for Senator Alston says the new rules are yet to take effect.
WA GOVERNMENT QUESTIONS BLACK DEATH FIGURES
The West Australian government says figures relating to Aboriginal deaths in custody are open to interpretion, and don't give a true picture of the situation.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Social Justice Commissioner Mick Dodson says the government has failed to implement several recommendations from the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody.
He says there've been 16 deaths in custody in Western Australia in the past seven years, and the number of juveniles killed in police pursuits in WA is much higher than other states.
But Justice Minister Kevin Minson says only half that number were deaths in prison or police lock-ups and only two of those were suicides.
HOWARD DEFENDS PURSUIT OF FREE TRADE
The Prime Minister has defended the drive for free trade in the Asia-Pacific region, saying it will give direct benefits to Australians.
APEC leaders, at their summit in Manila, have vowed to continue liberalising trade.
Mr Howard says reducing trade barriers in the world's fastest growing region will mean more jobs, higher living standards and a better future for young Australians.
He says if it wasn't for that goal, he wouldn't have Australia in APEC.
The Prime Minister returns from the Philippines today.
BLACKHAWK INQUIRY TOLD DEFENCE UNIT IS IN CRISIS
The Blackhawk Inquiry has been told the unit involved in the army's worst peace time accident will become defunct if staffing issues aren't resolved.
Lieutenant Colonel Tony Fraser, the unit's commanding officer, will continue giving evidence today to the inquiry into the Blackhawk disaster which killed 18 soldiers in June.
Two helicopters collided during a counter terrorism exercise near Townsville.
Colonel Fraser has told the inquiry the fifth aviation regiment was in crisis, morale was low, there was a shortage of experienced pilots and if the tide wasn't turned, the unit would be defunct.
He said while counter terrorism exercises were the top priority, more practice was needed, but could only be done at the expense of other activities because of understaffing.
MALAYSIAN PM GUARDED ON RACE DEBATE
At the close of the APEC leaders' summit in Manila, Malaysia's Prime Minister has clarified his country's position on the race debate in Australia.
Doctor Mahathir Mohamed says he won't bring up the issue with the Australian government, but Malaysia's silence doesn't mean he's not thinking about it.
He said Malaysia doesn't think the views of one person represents the views of the Australian government, however he did stress Malaysia does have an opinion on the matter.
HOWARD RETURNS FROM APEC SUMMIT
John Howard is already planning his strategy towards helping APEC to achieve its goal of free trade over the next 15 to 25 years.
The Prime Minister returns from the Philippines today, intending to tell Australians about the benefits of Asia-Pacific free trade.
The APEC summit ended with the leaders vowing they're determined to sustain trade liberalisation.
Mr Howard said it would be very hard for APEC to achieve its goal of Asia Pacific free trade, but there was movement and specific market benefits were starting to come from Asia.
He says he'll make trips to China, Malayasia and Singapore in the first half of next year.
DAMAGE BILL RISING IN COFFS FLOOD AFTERMATH
Damage caused by the weekend's flash-flood in Coffs Harbour could run as high as A$100 million.

The central business district was innundated by more than two metres of water at the peak of the flood on Saturday night, with initial reports showing at least 100 businesses, 500 houses and 300 cars were damaged.
The New South Wales Government has announced disaster relief, which will help the city council repair infrastructure damage, but will provide little comfort to the domestic and commercial sectors.
